units.title: Unit 37 — Health and medicine
learningObjectives: Discuss health maintenance using natural expressions for diet, exercise, strength and stress.
Distinguish the language of a medicine dose from a course of treatment and report responses safely.
Describe illness severity, duration, recovery and complications with idiomatic collocations.
Recognise British-English informal expressions and distinguish literal medical meanings from figurative usage.

items.example: Many older residents continue to enjoy good health well into retirement.
items.note: Enjoy good health is a natural way to describe having generally good health.

items.example: Short outdoor breaks may help employees reduce stress levels during busy weeks.
items.note: Reduce is commonly paired with stress levels; it does not promise to eliminate stress.

items.pt: recuperar ou desenvolver a força física
items.example: After several inactive months, Lara began swimming to build up her strength.
items.note: Build up describes gradual improvement rather than an immediate increase.

items.example: The physiotherapist encouraged him to do plenty of exercise within his limits.
items.note: The natural verb is do exercise, not make exercise; exercise is generally uncountable here.

items.example: Do you regularly do sport, or do you prefer walking for exercise?
items.note: Do sport is common in British English; play sport is also possible in some contexts.

items.example: The instructor began with gentle exercise before introducing more demanding movements.
items.note: Gentle describes low-intensity activity suitable for gradual progression.

items.pt: ter cuidado com o que se come
items.example: He tries to watch what he eats when travelling for work.
items.note: Watch what you eat means pay attention to food choices, not literally look at food.

items.example: She did not want to go on a diet but decided to cook more often at home.
items.note: Go on a diet means begin a particular eating plan; a diet also means what a person normally eats.

items.example: The researchers are studying how the immune system can build up resistance to certain infections.
items.note: Build up resistance refers to increasing the ability to withstand something over time.

items.example: A balanced diet includes a suitable mix of nutrients and food groups.
items.note: Balanced collocates with diet to suggest appropriate nutritional variety.

items.example: The coach recommended a sensible diet rather than an extreme eating regime.
items.note: Sensible diet describes reasonable, sustainable eating choices.

items.example: After several consultations, the patient was diagnosed with a medical condition requiring monitoring.
items.note: Diagnose someone with a condition names the condition identified by a clinician.

items.example: The surgeon explained why she might need to have an operation next month.
items.note: Have an operation is the usual patient-centred phrase; make an operation is incorrect.

items.example: The specialist decided to prescribe a course of medication after reviewing the test results.
items.note: A course of medication is treatment taken over a defined period; prescribe is the clinician’s action.

items.example: The patient responded well to treatment and gradually regained mobility.
items.note: Respond well to treatment refers to a positive reaction or improvement.

items.example: The doctors expect her to make a full recovery after rehabilitation.
items.note: Use make a recovery, not do a recovery; full stresses complete recovery.

items.example: The pharmacist warned the customer not to exceed the recommended dose.
items.note: Exceed means take more than the stated maximum; recommended dose is a standard label expression.

items.pt: tomar uma dose excessiva de medicamento
items.example: The leaflet explains what action to take if someone may have taken an overdose.
items.note: Take an overdose means consume a potentially harmful excessive quantity of a substance.

items.example: Some patients suffer side effects even when they follow the prescription correctly.
items.note: Suffer side effects refers to unwanted effects of a medicine; not everyone experiences them.

items.example: The clinical team recorded any adverse reactions reported during the study.
items.note: Adverse reactions is a formal medical combination for harmful or unwanted responses.

items.example: The nurse recorded the time at which the child received a dose of medicine.
items.note: A dose is a measured amount, unlike a course, which extends over a treatment period.

items.example: After the injury, the runner completed a course of physiotherapy.
items.note: Course of physiotherapy means a planned series of sessions, not a single appointment.

items.pt: um ciclo de tratamento com antibióticos
items.example: The clinician prescribed a course of antibiotics when a bacterial infection was confirmed.
items.note: Course indicates a prescribed treatment period; antibiotics are not suitable for every illness.

items.example: Mira stayed home because she had a streaming cold and could barely stop sneezing.
items.note: Streaming cold is a vivid, informal British-English expression involving a runny nose.

items.example: He struggled to shake off a cold that had lasted longer than usual.
items.note: Shake off a cold means recover from it; it is an informal phrasal expression.

items.example: Following the difficult winter, her grandfather remained in poor health.
items.note: In poor health describes an ongoing unfavourable state of health.

items.example: The report describes measures to limit the spread of an infectious disease.
items.note: Infectious describes a disease caused by an agent that can spread between hosts.

items.example: A specialist centre provides support for families dealing with a rare disease.
items.note: Rare describes a condition that occurs infrequently; it does not mean untreatable.

items.example: Researchers continue to seek treatments for an incurable disease affecting a small population.
items.note: Incurable means no cure is currently available; symptoms may still be treatable.

items.example: Many people manage a chronic disease with ongoing medical care.
items.note: Chronic describes a long-lasting condition, not necessarily an immediately severe one.

items.example: The rescue team transferred the critically ill patient to a specialist hospital.
items.note: Critically ill indicates a very serious, potentially life-threatening medical state.

items.example: After the accident, the cyclist was fighting for his life in intensive care.
items.note: Fight for your life is used when survival is in danger; person and possessive change with context.

items.example: The patient fell into a coma after sustaining a severe head injury.
items.note: Fall into a coma describes becoming unconscious in this prolonged medical sense.

items.example: The family were relieved when their relative finally came out of a coma.
items.note: Come out of a coma means regain consciousness after a coma.

items.example: The emergency team responded to a call about a massive heart attack.
items.note: Massive intensifies the seriousness of a heart attack in non-technical reporting.

items.example: The memorial reflected on the scientist’s untimely death at the height of her career.
items.note: Untimely death means a death occurring earlier than expected or fitting.

items.example: Better preventive care can reduce the risk of premature death from some illnesses.
items.note: Premature death emphasises dying earlier than the expected lifespan.

items.example: He cancelled his trip because he had developed a nasty cold.
items.note: Nasty is informal and emphasises how unpleasant an illness feels.

items.example: The presenter missed the meeting because of a heavy cold.
items.note: Heavy is a conventional intensifier with cold; it does not refer to weight.

items.example: A dose of flu kept several members of the cast away from rehearsals.
items.note: A dose of flu is informal British usage for an unpleasant bout, not a measured medicine dose.

units.title: Unit 38 — Criminal justice
learningObjectives: Use accurate collocations to describe offences, criminal responsibility and sentencing decisions.
Distinguish custody pending trial from a custodial sentence and a completed sentence.
Report court proceedings with precise verbs for testimony, verdicts, appeals and compensation.
Interpret common-law legal expressions without treating jurisdiction-specific concepts as universal.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: Several officials were criticised when the fraudsters appeared to escape punishment.
items.note: Escape punishment means avoid a penalty for wrongdoing, not escape from a prison.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: Under the ruling, the defendant will receive a custodial sentence rather than a fine.
items.note: A custodial sentence normally involves detention or imprisonment; especially common in UK legal English.

items.pt: cometer uma infração de menor gravidade
items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The report compared penalties for people who commit a minor offence.
items.note: Commit is the ordinary verb for an offence; minor refers to comparatively low seriousness.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The authorities decided to put the former official on trial for corruption.
items.note: Put someone on trial means begin formal legal proceedings against them.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The court found the accountant guilty after examining the financial records.
items.note: Find someone guilty is a verdict about criminal responsibility; the outcome follows the evidence.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The defendant was given a sentence of twelve months after the hearing.
items.note: Give a sentence is often seen in the passive, be given a sentence.

items.pt: cumprir a pena até o fim
items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: He was required to serve out his sentence rather than receive early release.
items.note: Serve out a sentence means complete the full period imposed, without early release.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The prison considered the inmate’s good behaviour when reviewing his eligibility for early release.
items.note: Good behaviour describes satisfactory conduct in custody and may matter when considering release, depending on the legal system.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: New DNA evidence revealed a miscarriage of justice in a case from the 1990s.
items.note: A miscarriage of justice is a wrongful legal outcome, notably the conviction of an innocent person.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: Several executives will face trial over the alleged misuse of funds.
items.note: Face trial means be due to undergo criminal proceedings; it differs from face a penalty.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The defence argued that the decision had rested on unreliable evidence.
items.note: Unreliable evidence cannot safely be trusted, irrespective of whether it is relevant.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The journalist said that the arrest was based on trumped-up charges.
items.note: Trumped-up charges are fabricated accusations; the phrase implies deliberate dishonesty.

items.pt: taxas de criminalidade em forte alta
items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: City leaders faced criticism over soaring crime rates in several districts.
items.note: Soaring describes a steep rise; crime rates measure crimes relative to a population or period.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: Investigators worked for years to bring those responsible to justice.
items.note: Bring someone to justice means make a suspected offender answer for wrongdoing through legal processes.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The court considered extenuating circumstances before determining the penalty.
items.note: Extenuating circumstances may lessen blame or punishment but do not erase the offence.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The lawyer referred to the defendant’s deprived childhood during sentencing.
items.note: Deprived suggests a serious lack of economic or social advantages.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The court requested an assessment of whether the accused was fit to stand trial.
items.note: Fit to stand trial concerns capacity to participate in proceedings, not whether a person is guilty.

items.section: A · Crime, sentencing and public debate
items.example: The defence presented mitigating circumstances for the judge to consider.
items.note: Mitigating circumstances is a close alternative to extenuating circumstances.

items.example: A key witness provided a detailed account of events during the hearing.
items.note: Key means especially important to establishing the facts of a case.

items.example: A former employee agreed to give evidence during the investigation.
items.note: Give evidence means present testimony in a legal proceeding, especially UK English.

items.example: The judge decided to adjourn the trial until the expert could attend.
items.note: Adjourn a trial means pause proceedings until a later date or session.

items.pt: manter sob custódia até o julgamento
items.example: The court decided to remand the defendant in custody pending the next hearing.
items.note: Remand in custody is pre-trial detention, distinct from serving a prison sentence.

items.example: After deliberation, the jury returned a unanimous verdict.
items.note: Unanimous means all relevant decision-makers agreed on the verdict.

items.example: The jury found the driver not guilty of the most serious charge.
items.note: A not-guilty verdict means guilt was not established to the required standard; it is not proof of factual innocence.

items.example: Prosecutors must prove the criminal charge beyond reasonable doubt in that legal system.
items.note: Beyond reasonable doubt describes a demanding standard of criminal proof in common-law systems.

items.example: The director denied all knowledge of the falsified invoices.
items.note: Deny all knowledge of something means assert complete ignorance of it.

items.example: The defence claimed that the witness was unreliable because the accounts kept changing.
items.note: An unreliable witness gives testimony that may be inaccurate or untrustworthy.

items.example: The judge decided to dismiss the case because the claim lacked a legal basis.
items.note: Dismiss a case means end it without granting the claim or proceeding further; exact effect depends on jurisdiction.

items.example: The court found in favour of the residents in the civil dispute.
items.note: Find in favour of someone means decide a legal dispute for that party; common in civil cases.

items.example: The court awarded damages to the injured pedestrian.
items.note: Award damages means order monetary compensation, usually in a civil case.

items.example: The legal team decided to contest the verdict through the appropriate procedure.
items.note: Contest a verdict means challenge a court decision; procedural options vary by system.

items.example: The appeal court overturned the verdict after finding a procedural error.
items.note: Overturn a verdict means reverse an earlier judicial decision, typically on review.

items.example: The witness is due to appear in court next Thursday.
items.note: Use in court, not on court, when describing attendance in legal proceedings.

items.example: The victims said that justice had been served after the final ruling.
items.note: Justice has been served is an evaluative phrase, not a guarantee that every legal outcome is fair.

items.example: The accused is expected to stand trial early next year.
items.note: Stand trial means undergo legal proceedings; it is not the same as simply attending court.

items.example: The jury delivered a guilty verdict on one of the counts.
items.note: Guilty modifies verdict; this is distinct from a sentence deciding the penalty.

items.example: The jury reached a not-guilty verdict after reviewing the evidence.
items.note: A not-guilty verdict means the criminal allegation was not proven to the required standard.

items.example: The company was advised on how to contest a court decision under the applicable rules.
items.note: This broader expression can apply to a decision, even when it is not technically a jury verdict.
